channel.title: RTW with BoB
channel.description: A travel blog about biking from Europe to South Africa

item.title: Debrief
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

The end was a bit anticlimactic. How could it not be? What could live up to years of accumulated struggle and effort and longing?

It has all come back very quickly. I’m at the gym daily - a soft landing for a body used to 8+ hours of exercise a day. Driving to the supermarket. Produce gleaming, large and unnervingly regular. Before, Landcruisers meant ministers and business magnates. Here, old mate’s off for a weekend camping. I don’t want to forget, but it’s hard to live split between two worlds.

Two things I took away.

Firstly, Africa is diverse. In language and religion, both colonial and native. In landscape: from the snow in Morocco’s towering Atlas mountains to the stiflingly humid Liberian rainforest. In culture. Just in Nigeria, I experienced both the hyper-capitalist chaos of Lagos and the understated hospitality of the Muslim east during Ramadan.

Secondly, kindness is human and universal. No matter where you go, people want to help. In more reserved places, they might need a little encouragement, but it’s magical watching a closed and wary face transform instantly into a smile at the chance to lend a hand. 90% of this needs to go to these humble helpers. A million tiny nudges moving me forward. Keep an eye out - I’ll be posting their stories here soon.

As expected, the trip changed me in unexpected ways. For a long while, paradoxically as an introvert, I struggled with loneliness. I got tired of the same shallow conversations, missing the deep ease and self-evidence of real friendship. I pushed myself to talk more. But the solution was actually developing this deep relationship with myself. Something that only solitude could teach me was missing.

I also learnt to better defend myself. I realised how far I’d come when, 10 minutes after a massive shouting match with corrupt porters on the boat to Equatorial Guinea from Cameroon, I felt totally calm. No jitters at all. The fight and ferocity rose instantly when needed and subsided just as quickly. I hope the continent’s vibrant life never leaves my veins. Apart from the malaria.

Thanks for accompanying me on this magnificent journey - maybe time for a little one of your own?

J&BoB

item.title: The end of the road
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

I started the final stretch to Cape Town feeling extra tired and looking extra homeless. The previous day’s battle had drained all my reserves, but the sight of the iconic table mountain in the distance filled the tank just enough to keep going. The destination was the Cape of Good Hope, the most south-western point of Africa. Cape Agulhas, the southernmost point of Africa, would have probably been more appropriate, but it was 400km away and I was too bloody tired.

With 30km to the cape, I heard a giant crack and the pedals went loose - the chain had snapped. And the derailleur jockey wheel was gone. And a spoke had ripped through the rim. I bodged a fix and managed to limp ahead, with the back brake disconnected to give more space to my wobbly wheel. Fitting, given the trip’s inauspicious start nearly 2 years ago.

I struggled and sweated my way to the cape, as if my body knew the end was coming. Not wanting to ride a single km more than necessary, I’d arranged for my uncle to come and pick me up. But with my phone broken I wasn’t able to warn him about the delay. I arrived more than an hour late and couldn’t find him. I sat and looked out at the bay, trying to process all that I’d seen and experienced - an impossible task - as a stream of tourists flowed past me to the lookout for photos. Somehow the lack of fanfare seemed fitting for a trip that had always been so deeply personal.

Eventually, I got up and found my uncle. To mark the end of the trip with an appropriate amount of suffering, I decided to carry BoB up the hundreds of steps to the lighthouse. This time I awkwardly answered a bunch of questions and even got a round of applause. But I was cooked and ready to hop in the car, have a shower and jump into bed.

The rest of my time in Cape Town was largely uneventful. My aunt fed me relentlessly and I gained 5kg. I did a few tourist things. I reconnected with a few cyclists who’d also finished their Africa journeys. I slept a lot. Staying with family was wonderful but the sudden lack of 100% freedom grated at me.

Then I packed BoB into a box and boarded my flight. One among hundreds on their way home.

Well fed and watered, J&BoB

item.title: Through the Northern Cape
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

I crossed the border slightly hungover into the beautifully desolate northern cape of South Africa. The riding was tough with corrugated gravel roads, strong headwinds and icy mist. There were few people but a lot of wildlife. Brightly coloured birds flocked and meercats rushed into their burrows as I approached. It took me a while to realise that the squeaking I was hearing wasn’t BoB, but the warning calls of mice in their burrows. This part of South Africa is famous for its wildflowers and, while I caught hints of them, they’d unfortunately come early this year.

The towns that I passed through matched the desolate landscape. Tiny beach town. Bleak and rusty. People were begging outside the supermarkets. They are sustained by tourism and mining, both of which had recently taken a hit. Peter, the owner of a guest house I stayed at, told me that the demountables were usually full of workers visiting the local diamond mine. With the massive drop in diamond prices, he had few customers and was desperately trying to scavenge what he could to keep the buildings from rusting away. Another local town, Koingnaas, hadn’t had power in four weeks. People were scavenging metal from the power lines.

Of course I came across a bunch of very kind people. Kobus and Engela paid for a hotel room and a couple of meals for me on a particularly cold day. André and Julian offered me tea and coffee and dinner at the entry post to the national park. Lizette and Dewald hosted me for a night and got me nice and tipsy on gin and tonics. Vicky gave me a coffee for free after I came back in panic after leaving my camera at her shop. Some of the generosity I’ve received seemed to come from a kind of solidarity among white people. I haven’t quite figured out how to process that yet.

Only 3 days to go to Cape Town! My mind has naturally started to process the trip as a whole. Trying to extract any big lessons or patterns. Despite my best efforts to enjoy what’s left, I’m also starting to think about what’s coming next. Worrying a little about guarding this sense of hard-won peace back in the busy western life.

Will let you know when I arrive!

Reflectively, J&BoB

item.title: Homecoming in Oranjemund
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

I encountered some magnificent scenery heading south from Maltahöhe. Wildflowers were in full bloom, coating the fields in yellow and purple. Clouds of dust left the sky so dark that I thought rain was coming.

While passing through a tiny village, I came across an enormous, rusting, mad-max construction in the middle of a field. I thought it was some kind of crazy radio communication device at first. I climbed it carefully, checking every step and saw that it was basically held together by rusty metal and prayers. Gerhard, who’s taking care of a neighbouring farm, said it was made by a local farmer, an ex-engineer who dedicated himself to making a single windmill to pump all the water for his farm and spent 30 years of his life working on it. Fascinating story.

On the way, I was showered in kindness once again. Piet, the avid cyclist who delivered the pedal for me, let me stay at his campground for free and lent me a mountain bike to ride with him. I thought I was cycling fit, but I had to give up after 1.5 hours and he was gone for another 2. Darnie, who works at the campground, helped me to fix my bags and let me stay in his camper for one night as well.

Finally, I made it to Oranjemund! I stayed at a local motel with a pub that, except for the afrikaans signs, could be straight out of the aussie outback. Through a friend of a friend of a friend, I got in touch with a lovely bunch of guys: Günther, Mike and Adrien and I already feel like family in my hometown. Mike is an absolute history buff. Apparently at some point the British visited the mouth of the nearby Orange river, looking for a more convenient place than Australia to dump their prisoners. They were lied to by some local farmers about the quality of the freshwater and continued south. If this hadn’t happened, Australia might have looked very different today!

This morning I visited the local museum and saw my parents in the phone books from the early 90s when I was born and the guys and I are heading down to the beach tonight for a barbie. Tomorrow I’ll be crossing the border to South Africa - the final border crossing. It’s going to be hard to leave.

Welcomed home, J&BoB

item.title: Pedal-less in Maltahöhe
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

Not too much to report since the last entry. I’m finally off the highway on a well graded gravel road. It’s been mostly flat with vast fields of dry grass on either side of the road. My right pedal snapped off, so I’ve been at a campground since Saturday waiting for a replacement. The rest is well needed though because my left knee has still been hurting. I really hope it won’t flare up too much over the next couple of weeks.

The kindness has been incredible too. As I crossed the Tropic of Capricorn, I met two families and they gave me a massive breakfast, a beer, a pile of snacks and even some cash! I hailed down another couple for some water, who also gave me a bunch of snacks. I’m incredibly touched. Martin, my host from Windhoek, had some spare pedals lying around and his friend is dropping them off to me on his way home.

The pedal should arrive late this arvo and I’ll be able to continue south on my way to Oranjemund. By next week I should be across the border to South Africa!

Too right, J&BoB

item.title: Corrugations to Windhoek
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

To avoid the frankly-scary highway riding, I chose a dirt road south to Windhoek. It was isolated, corrugated and sandy - tough on both me and BoB. BoB’s rack and seat supports snapped from the vibration and my knee pain flared up again.

Another challenge was finding food and water. Like Australia, Namibia is vast and sparsely populated, with distances more suited to cars than bikes. The roads are bordered by barbed-wire fences, punctuated by gates and dirt roads disappearing into the bush - farm houses well out of sight. Every hour or so a car would rush past in a cloud of dust. I managed to hail down some cars for water, but was running low on food after a couple of days. Luckily, there was a campsite with a small store and restaurant, where I wolfed down four plates of chips and a toasted sandwich.

Worried about my knee, I reluctantly continued to Windhoek on the highway. Along the way I passed luxury game and hunting resorts with electric fences, solar-powered security cameras and trucks restocking from game breeders. Seems to be big business here. All while black people walked the highways, unable to afford transport. The inequality is palpable.

In contrast, the hospitality I encountered on the way, and in Windhoek, was incredibly touching. I was offered a free stay at the Weaver’s Nest campground after beers and stories with owner Günther and his son. David and Diane from South Africa invited me to join them for red wine and nachos at the next campground. Crystal and Martin - and his parents Vera and Eckie - fed me to bursting and hosted me in Windhoek. Maria and Cronje invited me for dinner and great conversation. One bike shop gave me a free second-hand seat; another called every other shop in town hunting down parts for me. I’m lucky to have met such kind people.

I was mostly occupied with repairs, but found time to visit some monuments in Windhoek. Surprisingly, a lot were built by North Korea, who’ve made good business building monuments and statues around Africa. They have a distinctive style - noble bronze statues and murals full of pathos and grand narratives. If you’re interested, look up Mansudae Art Studio. Namibia has a bunch of their work.

Next stop is Oranjemund, where I was born!

Fresh and fit, J&BoB

item.title: Etosha
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

Namibia has been a big change. Suddenly, I have all kinds of luxuries available. It’s been nice to indulge a little but also a little frustrating, because at times I feel like I’m being funnelled into the tourist pipeline here. Locals either want to make money, or just feel like these are my standards as a foreigner. With so many people splashing cash here on short holidays, it’s hard not to feel cheap when I argue over prices. Though, I also don’t enjoy being charged three times the price.

Either way, I splashed out a little myself. I hired a car to visit the Etosha game reserve, which is quite famous in Southern Africa. It was really cool to see some animals up close and in person for the first time! Still, after two days of driving around in a car I was keen to reunite with BoB and get in closer contact with the environment again.

Just over a month to go before I arrive in Cape Town and a lot of ks to do, so it’ll be head down, tail up for a while again. Next stop is Windhoek, where I can get some parts for my bike and stay with a local host that I found online.

Reunited, J&BoB

item.title: Arriving in Namibia
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

Sorry for the long delay. I was quite sick in Equatorial Guinea and Gabon, had some bike troubles in Congo and had a lot of big riding days in Angola.

I just crossed the border from Angola into Namibia! It’s the second-last country of the trip and a gradual reintroduction into western life. There’s clean water from the taps, people speak English and I can buy peanut butter from the supermarket. I think I will eventually miss the challenge and chaos of Central Africa, but for the moment I’m enjoying the hell out of a red-velvet cake that I paid for by card.

Instead of trying in vain to catch up, I’m just going to continue from Namibia and write about what was in-between after I arrive in Cape Town. A lot happened in Equatorial Guinea and Gabon, so I promise it will be worth the wait.

Here are some pictures of the last few days of riding in Angola, where there are still some remnants of military equipment.

Comfortably, J&BoB

item.title: Languid Limbé
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

It was strange to be alone and on the road again after all that had happened in Yaoundé. The feeling quickly faded as I hit the fantastic yet completely empty highway that covered the first section to Douala. People apparently prefer the dilapitated old highway to avoid expensive police checkpoints. Another massive infrastructure project barely in use.

Passing through Douala, I spotted a church with striking, almost Gaudi-like, architecture called Heaven’s Gate - also the name of a cult whose members committed mass suicide in the late 90s. I wonder if they knew. I took some photos and some people started yelling and beckoning aggressively. I rode away. A few km later, a black Lexus came roared next to me, the driver, yelling, demanding why I was taking photos of his church. I braked hard and pulled over. Thankfully, he didn’t harass me further but it was a bit scary.

As the sun was setting, I arrived in a small town, halfway to Limbé. Searching for accomodation, I dodged a gaudy and expensive hotel, then a bar, whose aggressive owner showed me a tiny damp room filled almost entirely by a bed with a bare mattress, music shaking the walls. I refused. The last place in town was a brothel, with a lovely owner and reasonably priced, clean rooms. I took it.

The only problem was the giant steel door, connecting the corridor to the outside - the last girl would be leaving well after I planned to sleep. We decided that, since I was the only one there, she’d lock the door with my padlock when she left. She also told me not to respond or open the door in the night under any circumstances. Drunk men sometimes turn up in the night looking for company.

Around 6am I was woken up by a loud knocking on my door. Someone was yelling at me in pidgin, which I only half understand. Half asleep, I reflexively grunted an answer. For the next 15 minutes the knocking and shouting got louder and more aggressive. Fed up, eventually I opened my door. There was a guy in an office shirt who took a step back when he saw me. Turns out he was another overnight guest they’d forgotten about. He just wanted to get to work!

The rest of the ride to Limbé was uneventful if a little slow - I probably rested too long in Yaoundé. I found a comfy hotel in Limbé and got to work, first visiting Jodie, the girl I’d met in Yaoundé, who introduced me to a group of the volunteers at the local wildlife reserve. It was great to hang out and just chat with a group roughly my age. I also found out quickly that the boat to Malabo only leaves once a month. I had 10 days to kill until the next departure.

Malaria made a repeat appearance. Luckily, same as the last time, after 24 hours of medication I was feeling much better, though a mysterious intermittent nausea and a general malaise stuck around. I used the time to catch up on French practice, to work on the blog and took an elephant hike with the volunteers. We didn’t manage to see any (they’re usually more active at dawn and dusk), but did see lots of signs of them. They were all very well prepared with their hiking gear and pants tucked into their socks and very knowledgeable about the local fauna.

The hike got us talking about hiking Mt Cameroon. Sophia and Claire were keen so we organised a guide for a 3 day hike. The mountain is an active volcano which had a major eruption in 1999. The hike starts in Buea at 1000m for the peak at 4050m, so 3050m ascent in total over the first 1.5 days followed by a more relaxed descent. The hike was beautiful. We began in misty rainforest followed by grassy plains before reaching the rocky peak. On the way we stayed at two lovely lodges. The descent followed the old lava flows — a wide corridor of dark volcanic rock cutting through the green, scattered with small craters and odd outcrops of vegetation the lava had somehow spared.

Arriving back in Limbé felt amazing, until I realised that I’d left my wallet in one of the shared taxis we took down. Surprisingly calm, I immediately made plans to transfer money to my friends in exchange for enough cash to reach the next major town and have my new cards sent express. I then bumped into some other friends drinking with some of the local workers from the zoo, who had a totally different approach. We went back to the taxi rank and started talking. The drivers had seen us leave the taxi earlier and knew the driver. We gave him a call and it just so happened he was there at the rank. After a small negotiation he gave me my wallet back, cards and cash all intact. I gave him the cash inside and felt a little sheepish about how quickly I’d written it off. Sometimes I need reminding how things work here.

The next day I was back on the bike to Tiko, a nearby town and the departure point of the boat to Malabo, Equatorial Guinea.

Out of limbo,

J&BoB

item.title: Military intervention in Yaoundé
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

Yaoundé has a strange beauty despite the constant noise and crazy traffic. Every evening, the sun sets through the smog, bathing golden-red the hills, pock-marked with apartments, banana trees and towering state monuments. My hosts were lovely. An American/French couple volunteering at a local university. I had my first warm shower months and my clothes were blinding out of the washing machine. We ate dinner together in the evenings and discussed politics, culture and travel. A lovely respite.

As instructed at the border, I visited the General Delegation for National Security to get my visa sticker and stamp. After cycling there, I removed my boots and put on my embassy long pants and shirt, trying my best not to completely soak them with sweat. I walked in. They told me to go to the airport. I walked out. Sweaty pants and shirt off. I decided to leave the next day, visiting the airport on the way. Five minutes in total.

At least the whole thing wasn’t in vain, because while leaving I met someone living in Limbe, a city I planned to visit. We chatted briefly and exchanged numbers. Later that evening, she mentioned a cyclist who’d been missing for 9 days. It was Adrien, the Swiss guy I’d met at the border. His gps tracker had stopped for 4 hours just outside of town, moved into town at 80km an hour, almost certainly in a vehicle, and then had stopped in the ministry of defence.

I decided to postpone leaving and check it out. By my estimation, he’d either had an accident and was in the open-to-the-public military hospital, or he’d been taken by the military and was in custody. I needed to be careful, because my visa situation still wasn’t in order. The ministry of defence was on my way to the airport, so I made a plan. Visit the hospital first. If I found him there, great. If I didn’t, I would go to the airport and sort out my documents, then I would return and explore the ministry with my valid documents.

On Tuesday morning, it didn’t start well at the hospital. There is no central reception, so I hunted the corridors, packed with the sick and haggard, asking random staff if they’d seen a white patient. I visited multiple departments, emergency, surgery, vip care. Nothing. A Swiss doctor had been volunteering at the hospital, which just complicated matters. Luckily, I bumped into a formidable French doctor, who immediately instructed a nurse to help me find him. After searching the hospital, she was taking me to a clinic in the ministry, when we were stopped by some soldiers. One of the soldiers told me excitedly he knew exactly where he is.

We head into a military compound and immediately an officer chews me out for wearing shorts. The soldier, still smiling, leads me to a small field where I put on my pants half-discreetly. We move into a courtyard, with soldiers and civilians milling about. We approach some bars behind which I see a white, slightly waxy face. Instinctively, I approach the bars and start asking questions. Stop! No talking allowed. I’m told to sit and Adrien’s escorted out.

Surprisingly, we’re allowed to talk. He seems a bit stunned, but we get to business straight away. Who do I need to contact? Luckily, I brought a notebook and pen. He hurriedly writes down some names and numbers. His girlfriend. His dad. The embassy. Suddenly, someone arrived. I needed to go with them. Shit. It had all happened so fast, but this was exactly what I’d tried to avoid. Surrounded by the military without my papers in order.

I was brought in front of two men in sunglasses and fashionable grey suits. They chatted casually for five minutes. I waited, alert. Eyes firmly on the ground. With the same casual demeanour, they eventually began to ask questions. Firstly about my trip in general, with the usual canned answers. Then about corruption. Then about visas. “Do you always get a visa before arriving in a country?”. I tried to stop my hands from shaking.

I resisted the urge to obfuscate and told them the truth. I had an approved e-visa. At the border they told me to go to the airport for my visa. My only adjustment was saying the border was “missing a stamp” rather than “no longer a valid border” as they told me. At the mention of the e-visa, they seemed to relax. The conversation turned back to my trip. Why I’m not married and have no kids. They joked that I’m redirecting all the energy into riding and I genuinely laughed.

Later, Adrien was brought in. After 9 days detained, this was the first time he’d seen a higher-ranking officer. He told them passionately about the situation with the visa. At one point I tensed up as he, defending himself, said that he and I were in the same situation with the visa. But they seemed surprised that he had an e-visa at all and seemed to be on side. He mentioned he’d been sick for days and was losing weight. They offered him medical care and said he would have his phone that evening. Then they let me leave.

I got a beer to calm the nerves and contacted his friends and family. I didn’t think about it in advance, but his father was understandably suspicious of these whatsapp messages of dubious origin. He quite dryly thanked me for the information. Adrien’s girlfriend was more open and delighted to hear that he was safe and mostly sound. We organised for me to print a letter and bring it to him the next day. I had no idea if they would allow me back, but I would try. I put off talking to the embassy, because I thought they might tell me to stay out of it, stopping me from delivering the letter.

After that, I went to the airport. I briefly stopped during a passing storm, enduring the store owner insisting that I find him a white girlfriend. I chose to get wet. At the airport, the process was quite straightforward. First, a tag to pass security. Then the e-visa sticker. Photo. Fingerprints. The immigration officer seemed surprised, even though this was clearly a common occurrence. We had a brief, friendly conversation and he gave me a stamp for the date I crossed the border.

The next day, Wednesday, I went to visit again. I’d been sure to not offer any promises. After the frantic response the day before, I wasn’t sure they’d allow me back inside. I went back to the entry and handed over my phone and passport. They all recognised me and let me in with a smile. He was off getting treatment, however, and returned from the hospital over an hour later, looking much healthier. This time, we only had a few minutes together. Enough to hand over the letter and the news that everyone knew he was safe.

Afterwards, I went to the Swiss Embassy. Far from my expectations, the embassy staff were very appreciative to hear from me and had been working hard behind the scenes. I was offered a coffee with real milk (!) and the Consul, Roland, gave me his personal number. If things didn’t move soon, he said he might even just walk in with me. Another chat with Adrien’s girlfriend that evening. We were bonding quickly through this urgent, shared task.

In the courtyard Thursday morning, there were haggard-looking shirtless men holding cardboard signs saying “deserter” and “false agent”. People walking past occasionally taunted them, having a grand old time. Except the captors, of course. I needed to see the Colonel before visiting Adrien. He spoke excellent English and it was mostly chit-chat about travel while I cringed about the bag of fruit I’d brought slowly dripping on the office chair. He called someone to escort me. He didn’t arrive. He yelled out for someone to bring a walkie-talkie. Nobody responded. After two awkward minutes of yelling, during which I had no idea where to direct my gaze, finally someone came with the radio. No response to the radio. More yelling and someone was told to go and fetch the captain. More chit chat.

Eventually, the captain arrived and was mildly chastised. Then they chatted triumphantly, I assume about the new captives. After about 10 minutes, we left for the captain’s office. I waited 30 minutes outside. Obviously a power play. Eventually I entered the office and was told to sit. The captain and two obsequious underlings, one skinny, the other overweight with bulging eyes discussed the captives, all drinking beer. The captain downed the rest of his beer and, leering intensely, called a teenage girl in and asked for another beer. After it arrived and he’d had a swig, he escorted me, with another soldier, to Adrien. The captain was immaculately dressed, efficient and quite charming. He said I was free to return and visit whenever.

The captain immediately left, busy with more important matters. Adrien was comfortable in an air-conditioned hospital room. After discussing the essentials, we were free to just chat bikes, travel and his time being locked up; the soldier quietly sleeping in a chair in the corner. I imagine it was nice to just have a normal conversation again. Things had been rough, but also very interesting. At points the holding cell had 30 people in it, barely enough for them all to lie down. Mostly soldiers, they kept themselves and the cells very clean. There were also some heinous stories, told casually, about things they’d done while fighting in the far north. But for the details you’ll have to read Adrien’s book.

Friday, I went with a book and we chatted some more. Things seemed very relaxed this time. The guard had brought his PS4 and they were watching movies and playing games. The consul had visited and brought a pile of snacks, which Adrien tried to palm off onto me. Also a stack of cash. Almost worth getting detained if you’re Swiss. However long it would take, he was comfortable, if a little bored.

I got a text that night from the consul. Adrien was being released the next day. I arrived early and Adrien was clearly excited to leave. A little later, the mismatched envoy arrived. From jeans and sneakers of the consul’s driver, to the dress uniform of some of the military, others in suits and dark glasses and Adrien in his shorts with tan lines showing. The mood was conciliatory. The military explained at length why they needed to detain Adrien. Then the director of the hospital arrived and shamelessly hit on one of the nurses, putting his arm around her. He then held court on medical matters for 20 minutes. After another 10 minutes of awkward conversation the consul finally interrupted, suggesting that Adrien might be keen to leave. We stopped by the colonel’s office, who offered us expensive bourbon and wrote down his personal number on post-its and handed them out.

And then, Adrien was free! We threw our bikes in the back of a troop carrier and went to the consul’s place. Apparently, one of the captains had even asked the consul about getting a visa to Switzerland. We celebrated with pizza and beer. The consul offered for me and Adrien to stay at his place, which we gladly accepted. The air-conditioned room was magical. I even had a bath. That evening, we were invited to dinner with embassy staff. There was live music by a man in a sleeveless vest who would have been at home on a much bigger stage. It felt strange. After struggling for days for basic information and medical care, we were deciding which wine would best go with the food. Adrien was dumbfounded.

The next few days were relaxed for this odd thruple. Adrien and I definitely have completely different approaches to travel. He loves to ride. He told stories about ultra-endurance races. About hallucinating after days without sleep. Roland was shocked by our travel stories, but had stories of his own, about working in Istanbul, in Barcelona, in Azerbaijan. One night I made a big cous-cous and salad and we made cocktails. Adrien was back on his bike on Sunday, redoing the section he’d covered in the army van. He’d said he felt psychologically incomplete, having not ridden to his current location. No rest for the wicked.

And then, on Monday morning, after a week of madness, we parted ways. Me, heading west for Limbé, Adrien heading south for the Republic of Congo, and Roland, readying the embassy for the coming world trade organisation conference. It was a strange feeling to be on the road again. A little listless, even, after all the stress and clear plans. All that was left was to ride, and that’s what I did.

Miraculously free,

J&BoB

item.title: Struggle street to Yaoundé
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

After a brief rest stop in Banyo eating lots of salad and repairing my many accumulated punctures, I left for Tibati. The road was still bumpy, dusty and slippery. Still difficult to find food. One evening, I got a series of punctures that left me camping with only a handful of peanuts for dinner. I only reached the next town at midday and the best food I could find was a loaf of bread and a couple of tins of sardines. Stopping to eat or rest was frustrating because I was immediately surrounded by little flies that constantly try to crawl in your ears. I was also accosted once by a swarm of wild bees, collecting my precious sweat.

And precious it was because an unexpected side effect of the lack of food was the lack of salt. I began to cramp all over my body. Calves, hamstrings, hands, even abs. I was feeling quite ill by the time I arrived in Tibati. I made an electrolyte solution for myself and had a big salty dinner and was feeling fine in the morning.

I met Merlin who helped me find a little pocket of Christians serving breakfast. Even though he was a Christian, he was fasting without food or water as well for Lent. A bit more hardcore than giving up chocolate. He would do week-long stints at the community gold mine to make money. He’d also bring electronics with him to sell at the camp. Always hustling. Apparently the government has a monopoly on gold sales and sets a relatively low rate. Also, for every 10 bags you process, 8 go to the community, i.e. in someone else’s pocket. He said it was still worth it.

After Tibati, it was a newly-built, Chinese highway carved through the jungle down to Yaoundé. Occasionally, there was an optimistically signposted rest stop or emergency phone that didn’t exist or was shuttered. Clearly not built to an African plan. There was also almost no traffic on the road, which left a serene and smooth ride through the jungle.

The cramps returned. At one point I was squatting in the bush, doing my business and was hit by an enormous cramp in my abs. It was all I could do not to fall backwards into my boom boom. Suddenly the lack of traffic was more a liability than a benefit - nobody to hitch a lift from. I managed to limp into the next village and spent the next day in bed, drinking my isotonic drink and also took some malaria medicine to be safe. The rapid test in the clinic was negative, but you can never be too careful.

Another interesting observation was the change in culture crossing from Nigeria. I’d grown used to the noise of generators, the yelling, the laughter and the intrusiveness. Cameroon was the exact opposite. People kept their distance, often even avoiding eye contact. Some locals told me with pride that nobody would bother me in Cameroon if I minded my own business. It was also the first country that I saw individual houses in the countryside. Their familiarity shocked me a little. They wouldn’t look out of place in an Australian beach town, with wispy green lawns, full hedges and flower gardens. Up until now, people clustered into villages separated by open countryside. Perhaps this reflected a more individualistic and reserved attitude.

The traffic in Yaoundé was awful. Taxis lurk in the right lane, screeching to a halt at any moment to pick up a passenger. Sometimes another taxi will stop next to the first, trying to negotiate a better rate, or swerve in front of me and stop to pick someone up. I thought I had a hang of traffic in Africa by now, but I had a few close calls in Yaoundé.

I arrived to the warm shower and washing machine of my American/French hosts, thankful for some rest and western comforts after a lonely and difficult 6 weeks crossing Nigeria and northern Cameroon.

Scrubbed clean,

J&BoB

item.title: Race to the Cameroon border
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

After leaving Benue the good tar road turned to good gravel road turned to gnarly single track, which only motorbikes and the most patient of truckers dared to attempt. This all culminated in a day with over 2000m of elevation gain over loose gravel and dust. I only covered 50km and mostly pushed. But the air grew fresher and the sweat rash I’d developed slowly disappeared and the landscape opened up into beautiful broad grassy plains. The dusty, eucalyptus-lined roads wouldn’t look out of place in the outback in Australia. I arrived well after nightfall, with my phone strapped to my tent as a headlamp, invigorated by the renewed adventure of it.

One night I was hosted by Andrew, an evangelical priest who had recently been transferred into a tiny country town from Lagos. He had a big smile and a habit of responding with “that’s great!” multiple times to everything I said. His job wasn’t easy. In a small town the priest can have more power than the government. There was a half-finished church to complete and in that one evening three groups of people turned up with problems unannounced. The first, a teenage boy, shy and slightly trembling. He’d come to the town for work, but wasn’t being paid. He’d borrowed 500 Naira (30 US cents) to buy some soap to wash and couldn’t pay it back. Andrew listened while tapping at his ipad, gave him some food and told him to come with a family member the next morning to a funeral he was conducting.

For the Muslims, Ramadan was about to start and people had already started to fast to celebrate. This made finding food quite difficult as the region was remote and very Muslim. Early one afternoon, I arrived in a village hungry. The lone Christian let me cook noodles in his shop behind the counter. My stomach shrunk considerably over time and seemed to content itself with occasional sweets and energy drinks. I slept in a mosque one night where they didn’t speak English. Turns out I was eating in front of the guys on the first day of Ramadan! I was embarrassed, but they just smiled and offered me some food when they broke their fast later.

Sometimes, I ask people about local children’s stories. The men have been woeful so far, but I met a lovely woman who enthusiastically recounted the tale of a clever rabbit. I’ll very briefly summarise. The animal village wanted to have a town meeting outside of the village and had prepared a feast for afterwards. The rabbit said it had to run some errands and couldn’t come. When everyone left, the rabbit went and ate all the food and then put the shoes and droppings of one of the other animals outside the door. When everyone returned and saw their food gone, they blamed the animal and killed it. The moral of the story? Be clever like the rabbit if you want to get your way.

Crossing the border was straightforward, if a bit uncomfortable. The Nigerian immigration (one man) was friendly and stamped me out without problems. Not so in Cameroon. Officially, this border post hasn’t been open since COVID which meant no stamp or visa sticker. I was reassured it wasn’t a problem and told to get my visa Yaoundé, essentially travelling illegally. At the border I also met Adrien, a Swiss cyclist setting the record for a north to south traversal. He casually said he would be doing 300km per day!

Trying to save some money, I opted to withdraw it on the Cameroonean side directly, which is normally possible at the border. In this case, the nearest place was Banyo, 40km from the border. This meant riding a dusty, rocky road on an empty stomach for hours. When I finally arrived in Banyo, everything went wrong. My new SIM card’s internet didn’t work. The man’s son, who knew how to fix the internet, was breaking his fast and would come back in an hour. Two hours later the son returns and doesn’t know how to fix it either. I buy a second sim card, but the app denies multiple transfers. I was strangely calm, even though I was hungry. I can feel the months of accumulated travel changing me. Making me tougher. More patient. Eventually, I send money to the guy’s personal account and he gives me the cash for a fee. I buy myself fish and chips and find a hotel. Bliss.

Mildly illegally,

J&BoB

p.s. I went a bit overboard with the landscape photos. It was really beautiful.

item.title: 15 minutes of Nigerian fame
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

My closest brush with fame came after leaving Abuja. Emmanuel is an overland cyclist like me. Unlike me (<3 you mum), he has a massive online following. He’s heading to the USA via Europe. I had met him briefly under blazing sun on the highway in Liberia. He happened to be in Abuja and contacted me just as I was leaving, so I stayed with him and we had dinner together.

He looked tired. He’d just had his European and US visas denied, despite clear evidence of his journey and following. Someone had also leaked his phone number and he was regularly getting calls from righteously furious fans, helpfully offering to harass the embassies for him. He was relentlessly positive, though. To keep the content flowing, he was planning to ride a motorcycle around Africa. At some point, he told me that he was posting five or six times a day. A real hustler.

I left early the next morning, keen to finally make progress. People started to recognise me and call out on the road. He’d posted a picture of us that morning. As I entered Benue, Emmanuel’s home state, the attention increased tenfold. People pulled up ahead of me, sometimes dangerously, beckoning me to stop for a selfie. Everyone wanted a little bit of my time. Two minutes per selfie with 100 people is over three hours - I had to ignore most requests. People were sometimes upset. It’s surely cultural, so no judgement, but Nigerians will raise their voice three or four times if they don’t get your attention. Regularly being yelled at from multiple sides with escalating volume triggered some primal stress in me, however unintentionally.

Crossing the Benue river was chaos. Boats crammed with people, motorbikes and even cars jostling and bumping their way across the river. I negotiated a boat across, despite the help of a local official who insisted on accompanying me and did nothing to prevent the drivers charging me five times the price. A local influencer hailed down my boat and got in. He’d seen Emmanuel’s post and wanted to guide me across - a bit late, as I was already mid-river. On the five minute trip, he spent most of the time on his phone. When I invited him to lunch after some pictures, he said he needed to return. Some poor child somewhere probably needed a good influence. The official then asked for a tip. For trying to rip me off. Bloody audacious.

I arrived in Emmanuel’s town late one evening and a crowd immediately formed. Someone offered to get me a beer but never returned. Another started rattling off geography facts. Impressed, I engaged - he returned ten minutes later with a handwritten résumé asking for a job. Endless requests for selfies. Tired and overwhelmed, I followed some guys in the dark to Emmanuel’s parent’s place. I was immediately swamped, phone torches in my face. The family were very generous, offering me some dinner and a comfy bed. My morning sleep in was short-lived though and I was summoned outside with multiple knocks on the door to present myself to all the people who’d come to welcome me. People preferred watching to talking. I ate my breakfast with a huge crowd, mostly in silence. I don’t want to seem bitter or unappreciative - there was no malice or selfishness involved, just an unavoidable misunderstanding. I gave a grand speech of appreciation to great applause and rejoined the relative solitude of the road with a big sigh of relief.

After Zaki Biam, I took a shortcut on a lovely dirt road, which, similar to before, had only very recently become passable. I rode through small, abandoned villages full of burnt-out buildings. It led me to Sai, where I stopped for a break. A crowd formed and the residents begged me to tell the world about their struggle. Bandits were burning their homes and kidnapping people. Videos were circling of young American missionaries with glistening smiles calling out the Nigerian government’s inaction. They clearly wanted the same from me, but it was too risky. I promised to spread the word instead. Some people’s lives are unbearably difficult in this country.

As I left Benue, my fame thankfully ended. I still had about 300km to travel and only a few days to get to the border.

The unfamous,

J&BoB

item.title: Sketchy riding to Abuja
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

With the threat of kidnapping unavoidably in mind, the trip from Esie to Abuja did not start auspiciously. A soldier chased me down on the back of a moto-taxi and interrogated me - not to protective, but suspicious. What was I doing there? Where was I going? After we established I wasn’t a spy, he let me go, but told me the area was dangerous. A few kilometres later, a packed sedan overtook me and swung across the road. This time, the “community police” - a group of men keeping the community safe. Again, questions and suspicion. Eventually they calmed down and let me pass with smiles and waves.

Later that day I passed a church ringed with spiked walls and barbed wire - I took a photo, and a man screamed at me that I had no right. I calmed him down and moved on. A little later, I stopped for a quick rest in an open-air church, essentially a gazebo with some chairs in it, and sat doing my Duolingo. Five minutes later, more community police, this time more aggressive. They demanded to see my ID. I refused. They told me to wait for the police. I said I wanted to leave and started wheeling my bike away. One of them grabbed it. It turned into a shouting match, until their boss arrived - not an official, but I showed him my passport anyway to get out of there. He sent me up the road to the military commanding officer, who didn’t give a shit and let me go.

I’ve travelled quite a bit and never experienced this before. People are often scared for me, never of me. Usually when people tell me the surrounding area is dangerous, they’re either being protective of the lily-white soft-soled visitor or are a bit biased about their neighbours. This felt entirely different and left me on edge. A couple of times people ran away when I came too close. The fear was palpable. Luckily for me, the kidnappings and violence had peaked in October 2025, after which the military was sent in. There was certainly a massive military presence - AK-47s, armoured vehicles, checkpoints every few kilometres from various branches of the military and police. On their guard, but polite. Most refused photos but some absolutely insisted.

With heightened senses, I made sure to pass through Lokoja - previously the centre of kidnappings in the area - in the middle of the day. Crossing the Niger river was a huge relief. Soon after, I reached the highly-secured Federal Capital Territory around Abuja and was finally safe. I was tired. Not only of fear, but of the suspicion that came with it. A couple of times I deliberately stopped because I thought I was being followed, mistaking curious motorbikers as spotters for the kidnappers. I don’t regret being cautious, but it was exhausting.

Abuja was both a huge contrast to what I’d experienced and a contrast in itself. Like many other purpose-built capitals, it feels like the embodiment of a retrofuturistic 1950’s dream-turned-nightmare. The centrepiece of the modest city centre is three massive highways lined with tessellated “luxury” residential estates, with some suburbs for the poor tucked in between. It’s not quite the hyper-luxury flex-fest of Lagos. Slightly more old money in the mix.

I didn’t ask, but my first contact in Abuja gave off exactly that vibe. She owns a successful business giving music lessons to the city’s wealthy and, in a familiar pattern, was very kind and generous to me. She didn’t have space to host me, so I stayed on the floor of her employee’s tiny tin-and-wood house. I was given free meals at the café and a driver and air-conditioned Lexus for a day of visa hunting - another shocking contrast.

A devout Christian, my host took me to choir practice that evening, where the choir leader openly ridiculed two girls for their lack of enthusiasm. When I casually praised his singing the next day, the school’s music director mocked my taste. I decided to find my own place after that and other overreaches. Rich Nigerians can be horribly dismissive of the poor. I’m glad I moved on, because near the hotel I met HEARTMAN, a talented beat maker and rapper. I got to sit and listen to some of his tracks with him. He said he’d recorded most of it on his phone. Incredible.

My main task in Abuja was to get my visa for Equatorial Guinea - a notoriously secretive and closed country whose consulate here is one of the few places that actually grants visas to travellers. Unfortunately, I arrived on a Thursday evening, confirmed the required documents on Friday, and was left with Monday for the application. My 30-day Nigerian visa ticking down with a solid 700km still ahead, I was itchy to leave. But consulates set their own cadence and the ambassador of Equatorial Guinea was especially busy this week.

By Friday I’d packed my things and was waiting outside the embassy with the guards, hoping to get my visa and hit the road immediately, which irritated the embassy staff. While waiting, a shifty guy in wraparound mirrored sunglasses came over and knowingly asked if I was from the CIA. After I refused his request for my phone number and he hassled me further, the guards told him to piss off - after which he stalked the streets a bit before calling the police, who arrived demanding my passport. They went into the consulate to confirm my story, likely irritating the staff further. After the police left apologetically, I was invited inside.

The ambassador’s secretary - who seemed to be largely running the show - filled out the visa. She said she wanted to go home and would let the ambassador know later. I paid directly into her account and she made it fairly clear she’d like an extra gift. When I rushed downstairs and brought her seashells from Côte d’Ivoire, she was visibly disappointed. But the visa was done, she wanted to go home, and she waved me out with a wry smile. Still no bribes given after over a year in Africa!

In fact, I didn’t leave straight away, and spent one more night in Abuja thanks to a chance message from another cyclist. But that will have to wait for the next entry.

Overcapitalised,

J&BoB

item.title: Sweating to Esie
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

I left Lagos in the late afternoon, keen to put even a little distance between myself and its insanity. I quickly regretted it when I found myself on an empty highway at sunset with nowhere to stay. Even after more than a year in Africa, the talk of bandits, robberies and kidnappings made me nervous. Usually, people claim the neighbouring countries are dangerous and insist theirs is different. In Nigeria, for the first time, their nationalism is always followed by a “but…”.

As always, my nervousness was overblown. I found a church in a small village and stayed the night. In the morning, the pastor brought bread and chocolate milk for dipping. “Tea and bread” - a Nigerian staple. Later that day I broke a spoke. Godwin and his son gave me replacements for free. Nigerians are direct, in their requests and their kindness. I have never had so many people offer small gifts along the way. At times the attention felt oppressive. Nigeria was a good lesson in saying no.

The riding was tough. There is no decent road through to Abuja, so I cut across the countryside. It was lush and beautiful, but oppressively hot and humid, and the roads were dreadful. Conscious of my short visa, I rode long, sweaty days with little progress. I developed a sweat rash and BoB had his own collection of maladies.

Even in the countryside I passed countless checkpoints: army, vehicle inspection, police, forestry, even the navy, hundreds of kilometres from the coast. Local communities set up ad hoc checkpoints to shake down visitors. Essentially rent seeking, people said it was for the community. While taking it from other communities, of course. Luckily, as a sweaty white man on a bicycle, I was a spectacle and spared the extortion, even though I could better afford it than most. I also passed many churches and mosques, growing grander as the people grew poorer. Economically, such splendour built on the backs of the poorest on earth is a scandal. Psychologically, it makes sense. The poorer and more uncertain your life, the more religion offers a sense of control.

Towards the end of my journey I stayed with Simeon, an engineer with a master’s degree getting by as a contractor. When he was younger he scraped together money for a visa and flight to Europe. On arrival he discovered the visa was fake and was sent straight home, broke. He and many others told me that without connections, work is hard to find in Nigeria. For a good government job you often have to pay a bribe of many thousands of dollars, and sometimes still do not get it. He rented a small room in a family home. The landlord’s fourteen year old daughter had recently used a spare key to steal cash and building supplies from his room. I saw him in deep discussion with local police and church elders. He wanted justice, but not for her to be burned with hot irons or beaten. He did not want her arrested either, as she was the sole carer for her bedridden mother. Despite all this, he was glad to host me for the night. It is not easy in Nigeria. People say that often.

I had taken a detour to the National Museum in Esie, the first in Nigeria, where thousands of intricate soapstone figures were discovered centuries ago beneath some trees. The museum and local schools were closed due to the threat of kidnapping. The guard was alarmed by my bicycle helmet, mistaking it for a combat helmet. Once he realised I was a tourist, he called his boss, who gave me a free personal tour. I think he was glad to have something to do.

After many conversations about the safest route, I nervously set off for the capital, Abuja.

On our toes,

J&BoB

item.title: Lagos
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

Lagos is an enormous, sprawling city of 20 million people, the second largest in Africa. Everything here is done en masse. Cars. People. Animals. Buildings. All of it crammed into every nook and cranny. As with many places of such density, scams are rampant. I ordered doughnuts and watched as the final one “accidentally” missed the bag and fell back onto the pile. I bought a month’s data and got a day. When I argued, she said she bought it for a week. Prices varied wildly based on how vulnerable I looked to the seller. I quickly became less trustful and tougher, not a particularly natural or enjoyable role for me.

In contrast, some areas of the city are stomach-turningly rich. Rows of luxury apartment blocks with jetties and speedboats on the river. Luxury clubs with infinity pools. All in plain sight of those sleeping on the streets. I took a taxi that evening to meet a local friend-of-a-friend. The driver spoke rapturously of “dirty December”, when the Nigerian diaspora returns to Lagos to flex their foreign earnings. Like the cliché in the USA, I think he saw himself as a temporarily embarrassed millionaire, trying to win the game rather than change it. At the rooftop bar, beers were 7,000 naira. At a regular bar, they’re 1,200. It’s like paying fifty dollars for a Heineken in Australia. Absurd.

The cheapest hotel I could find was a “luxury” place (sorry for all the quotes, I’m feeling particularly sarcastic today), a microcosm of the surrounding city. My room looked out over the slums that encircled the hotel. The hot water didn’t work, but they called me sir while apologising. The breakfast was meagre, but was served by staff in crisp white shirts and bowties. Of course, there was also a pool and fitness studio.

One haven in the chaos is the Niké Art Gallery, absolutely stuffed with paintings and sculptures. I felt like I understood Nigeria better after seeing it through the eyes of a thousand artists. The effusive and theatrical Niké welcomed me and immediately dubbed me “the bicycle man”, introducing me as such to the gallery’s many guests, partly because I’m sure she forgot my name in the hubbub. I felt like a minor celebrity, but also like an object. Taking selfies, striking the requested pose, then being ignored the moment the photo was taken. I was just another flex. Later, Niké gave me a fan with her face on it and kindly offered for me to stay in her daughter’s apartment, still under construction, which I gladly accepted to avoid another night at the hotel.

I was glad to leave the city the next day, completely overwhelmed by its mess of activity and contradictions.

Classily divided,

J&BoB

item.title: Recovery and ride to Lagos
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

I passed broken down vans, verdant golf courses and people bathing in rivers on the immaculate new coastal road from Ouidah to Cotonou. That night, we went to a wine-and-cheese night hosted by a French expat in an apartment looking over this pristine waterfront. A far cry from sweating on the floor in Ouidah. Is it right to move so seamlessly between two worlds?

Then I got sick. Probably COVID. Luckily, I’d found a relatively cheap hotel with western food so I rested in comfort, extending my stay a few times. Once I realised that I also had malaria, I took the medication and recovered quickly. BoB and I were back on the road to Nigeria after this week of enforced rest, a little weak but good spirits.

I stopped by the capital Porto Novo and ended up drinking with some fisherman into the evening. As I followed two guys from the side of the road to a cheap hotel, a little drunk, it hit me how far I’d come from the trip’s first nervous steps. I realise that this might seem silly or reckless to some, but all I can say is that many months on the road fills you with an overwhelming certainty that things will be okay, a tolerance for discomfort and an excellent radar for bullshit in which I have full confidence.

The next day, the roads to the border were lined with stalls selling cheap fuel smuggled across the border. At one of the stalls, I met a fellow cyclist from Ghana with an absolutely tricked-out bike including inbuilt subwoofer. A true engineer. Thankfully, I crossed the border without any problems. On the road I met Tunde, who paid for a hotel for me. The first of many acts of generosity here.

On the way into the city the next day, I met a ton of people. Many asking for money or selfies, but others with no agenda. Susan has four kids, just got divorced and is very proud of the store that she’s running to support her family. Princess, selling routers, hit on me ruthlessly. White guys are definitely seen as a way to escape Nigeria. Promise tried to scam me while I was buying data. You’ve got to be on your toes here.

Lagos itself is pure chaos. The most populous city in the most populous country of Africa, there it just too much of everything at all times. Too many cars and motorbikes. Too much rubbish. Too many people. Too much noise. Entering the city, I passed a guy striding down the centre of the road, probably high, with an empty gaze, holding up traffic. I guided him off the road, breaking him from his single-minded focus and he collapsed, immediately unconscious. As I was rolling him onto his side, people yelled at me from all directions to leave him. That it was his fault. That he deserved it. This small act of kindness enough to make them uncomfortable. The other side of Nigeria.

I found a too-expensive hotel - nobody had answered my couchsurfing request in this city of 20 million, a first in Africa. Definitely a place of contrasts.

Dividedly,
J&BoB

item.title: Vodun days
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

Vodun is an animist religion in West Africa and the origin of the Voodoo traditions of the Caribbean and mainland America. It is celebrated every year on the 10th of January in Benin, where it is practiced by most people alongside Islam or Christianity. Lately, the festival has grown in popularity, partly due to massive investment by the current president and autocratic leader Patrice Talon, perhaps in an attempt to launder the country’s reputation a little after the coup attempt in late 2025.

The emphasis was very much on Vodun as holistic religion, emphasising its focus on peace and connection with nature, probably to counteract foreigner’s (and my own) ignorant association of voodoo with bloody sacrifice. I saw some impromptu sacrifices on the street by residents during the celebrations, but they were very much not on the official program, which was well typeset and had been broadcast for weeks over every imaginable form of social media. There were even, somewhat inexplicably, guys hired to ride bikes through the town with big banners during the festival.

As a well-organised, curated and somewhat sanitised cultural festival it was a massive success. The massive parties on the beach in the evening added some well-needed chaos back into the mix, with the heaving crowd happily flowing around the dozens of people sleeping on the sand. Police formed a line hundreds of metres long to stop any ill-fated attempts as swimming and armoured vehicles stationed at the entrances. The festival ended with a big ceremony in a brand new area with limited seating that we managed to sneak our way into with some quick thinking from my friends.

Seeing this very rich expression of centuries of religious practice reinforced to me how much (white) Australia is lacking in this regard. There’s a kind of dismissive approach to this kind of local culture as arbitrary and useless that I think is a bit misguided. One of many lessons.

Still exhaustedly buzzing after the festival, it was time to head to the economic capital Cotonou.

Bloodlessly,
J&BoB

item.title: Riding to Benin
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

After Lomé, I had an impromptu stay with Caroline’s friend Jean-Christophe in Aného, close to the border with Benin. I was originally just stopping by for a drink, but he was such an endless fountain of facts that I asked if I could stay the night. He’s been a consultant in the region for many years, mostly with breweries, and had a lot to say about everything from local politics to relationships to 60’s rock and roll. A very intelligent guy.

The rest of the ride to the festival in Ouidah was largely uneventful for a change. I managed to get myself lost, was redirected by some kids and subsequently chastised by a local leader for not having a guide and not introducing myself to the local authorities. He insisted that the local area was full of terrorists. Then, realising the implication about his leadership abilities, insisted that it was very safe despite the rampant terrorism. I meet big men like him quite often. The best thing to do is just smile, nod and fake a very infectious illness as soon as possible.

I arrived in Ouidah still feeling a little socially overwhelmed. The single night of solitude while camping hadn’t fully scratched my hermit’s itch. Unfortunately, Ouidah’s accomodation had long since been booked out for the festival. I had no plan at all about where I would stay, but was sure I would find somewhere to put my tent. Thankfully, Caroline organised a connection with someone in Ouidah. In fact it was her friend’s son’s friend’s nephew, so all in all my friend’s aunt’s friend’s friend’s son’s friend’s nephew. It’s crazy how far I’ve come with such loose connections.

Things got a little weird from there. Expecting just a little help finding a camp spot, I found out that, without informing me, the son had come all the way from Cotonou to guide me through the festival for the next few days. Originally, I found this very sweet, if a little forward and slightly restrictive, but later his uncle, who’d organised the whole thing arrived to talk, clearly drunk. Conversation came relatively quickly to compensation for the family, with the nephew looking on timidly in the background. Checkmate. In the end, I paid. Probably too much. This deliberate mixing of relationships and money is something I really detest, but I didn’t have much choice.

I sweated myself to sleep on my sleeping mat, excited about the first day of the festival.

Excitedly,
J&BoB

item.title: Lome circus
item.description:
Hi BoBers,

With my poor little introverted self feeling quite exhausted by the constant company, I left Accra after a tearful goodbye with the family, followed by one glorious, solitary night camping under a mango tree. After five mangos for breakfast, I crossed the border to Togo (totally straightforward) and arrived at Alice’s aunt’s friend Caroline’s place in Lomé.

She’s spent the last 14 years of her retirement there and, now in her late sixties, her house is a little oasis in the city—both in nature and French culture. The garden was dense with plants and the interior packed with art; tiny sculptures and paintings lurking everywhere. The walls were covered with a new exhibit she was preparing on the history of clothing for the local museum, her desk with cartons of cigarettes, and each room had a jam-jar ashtray filled with water. My occasional social smoking accelerated massively during our after-dinner conversations on the terrace (decelerating has been an ongoing struggle). We ate crêpes and cheese (!!), drank red wine, and bonded over a shared love of Terry Pratchett—she even had a custom miniature Discworld coffee table.

The closest I’ve come to being a tourist in a long time, we hired a tuk-tuk and toured Lomé. Full of vim and vigour, she chatted constantly with the driver. We shared an avocado sandwich on the beach and answered questions from a random guy curious about geography.

Caroline had close ties with the country’s only circus school which specialsed in stilt walking - a traditional performance art in Togo. We went to visit and they even let me have a go myself. The stilts flex as you walk, but by the end, sweaty and sore, I could manage a few small manoeuvres. Part of me wanted to drop everything and join the circus. Learning with your body feels far more natural than the dry study I do back home in front of a computer.

On my final evening, Caroline had a health scare that made it difficult to leave, but she insisted. With little time before the Voodoo festival in Benin, I hit the road—another separation from a fleeting, intense connection.

Enchanté,
J&BoB
